# Machine learning: models and algorithms {.unnumbered}

> *"Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful."* — George E. P.
> Box [@box1987]

This part corresponds to the fourth course of the master: the main families
of supervised learning algorithms. Part III built the framework — risk and its
estimation, cross-validation, regularisation, metrics, pipelines — around
linear models. This part fills it with the algorithms that every practitioner
is expected to know, and with the optimisation methods that fit them: how they
work, what they assume, when they fail, and how to compare them fairly.

The chapters follow the course's modules: gradient descent and its stochastic
variants, the optimisation engine behind most models; the distinction between
parametric and non-parametric models, which organises everything that
follows; naive Bayes, the simplest generative classifier; support vector
machines and kernels; neural networks, from the perceptron to the universal
approximation theorem; nearest neighbours, the model of the final project;
and decision trees and random forests.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this part matters for an AI engineer
Deep learning dominates images, sound and text, but most data in companies
still sit in tables, and on tables the algorithms of this part — gradient
boosting and random forests, regularised linear models, $k$-NN and kernel
methods — remain strong, cheap and explainable. More importantly, every idea
of deep learning appears here in its simplest form: stochastic gradient
descent and Adam, the bias–variance trade-off of flexible models, margins and
kernels, backpropagation, early stopping, ensembles. And whatever the model,
the engineer's job is the same: choose it by an honest comparison, not by
reputation.
:::

## What you will be able to do {.unnumbered}

1. Fit any differentiable model by gradient descent, stochastic and
   mini-batch gradient descent, momentum and Adam; prove when they converge
   and how fast; train online with `partial_fit`; read a training history and
   stop early (@sec-ch-mla-optim).
2. Tell parametric from non-parametric models, prove their convergence rates
   (fast but biased when wrong; assumption-free but slower, and cursed by
   dimension) and choose between them (@sec-ch-mla-parametric).
3. Apply Bayes' theorem without the base-rate fallacy and build naive Bayes
   classifiers of every variant — Gaussian, Bernoulli, multinomial, complement,
   categorical — with smoothing and calibrated expectations
   (@sec-ch-mla-nb).
4. Derive the support vector machine from the maximal margin to the soft
   margin, its dual and KKT conditions, and use kernels, with $C$ and $\gamma$
   tuned by cross-validation (@sec-ch-mla-svm).
5. Build, train and understand neural networks: the perceptron and its
   convergence, activation functions, backpropagation from scratch,
   initialisation, and what universal approximation does and does not
   promise (@sec-ch-mla-nn).
6. Classify with nearest neighbours: choose the distance, the scaling and $k$,
   abstain with radius neighbours, and explain the Cover–Hart bound and the
   curse of dimensionality (@sec-ch-mla-knn).
7. Grow, prune and read decision trees; reduce their variance by bagging and
   random forests; interpret forests with out-of-bag estimates and
   permutation importance (@sec-ch-mla-trees).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

Part III, especially risk and the Bayes classifier (@sec-ch-ml-intro),
preprocessing and pipelines (@sec-ch-ml-preprocessing), gradient descent for
least squares (@sec-gradient-descent), the bias–variance decomposition and
cross-validation (@sec-ch-ml-regularization), and classification metrics
(@sec-ch-ml-classification). This part does not repeat them: it links back and
recalls statements in one line where needed. Mathematics beyond Part III —
convexity, Lagrange multipliers, Taylor expansions with remainder — is
introduced where it is used.

## Graded practice {.unnumbered}

From this part on, every main section ends with a **Practice** block of three
exercises: **Easy** (apply the idea just seen, often by hand), **Medium**
(implement or vary it in code), **Hard** (a small open problem combining
several ideas, in the direction of the final project). Each has a collapsed
**hint** and a separate collapsed **solution**, with executed code, the
reasoning behind it and the typical mistakes. The end-of-chapter exercises
remain, as synthesis problems.

## Libraries and data used {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import sys, numpy, pandas, sklearn, matplotlib, scipy
print(f"The code of this part was executed with **Python {sys.version.split()[0]}**, "
      f"**scikit-learn {sklearn.__version__}** [@pedregosa2011], **NumPy {numpy.__version__}**, "
      f"**SciPy {scipy.__version__}**, **pandas {pandas.__version__}** and **Matplotlib {matplotlib.__version__}**; "
      "every output shown was produced by actually running it when the book was built.")
```

A small helper module,
[`mlalg/mlalgbook.py`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-engineering-handbook/blob/main/mlalg/mlalgbook.py),
reuses the figure style and palette of Part III and draws decision regions.
Algorithms are implemented from scratch in NumPy and checked against
scikit-learn; the interactive widgets are computed in Python when the book is
built and explored in the browser.

The data of the theory chapters are generated in the code (so that the truth
is known) or are public data sets with a clear licence that ship with
scikit-learn: the wine data [@aeberhard1992] and the Wisconsin breast-cancer
data [@wolberg1993] already used in Part III, Fisher's iris data
[@fisher1936; @fisher1936data] and the handwritten digits [@alpaydin1998], all
under CC BY 4.0. The project analyses the fruit measurements provided by the course,
whose licence is not declared: the handbook does not contain the file but
reads it from the companion repository, pinned to a commit, and checks what it
contains (@sec-fruit-data).

## Map of the part {.unnumbered}

| Chapter | Core topics | What the book adds |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-ch-mla-optim | derivatives and gradients, gradient descent, online, mini-batch and stochastic GD, constant and adaptive learning rates, `partial_fit`, training history, early stopping | steepest descent and finite differences proved, step-size theorem and condition number, unbiased mini-batch gradients and the $1/\sqrt T$ SGD bound, heavy-ball rate, Adam's bias correction, early stopping ≈ ridge |
| @sec-ch-mla-parametric | parametric and non-parametric models, how to choose | Gaussian MLE and misspecification (KL), histogram and kernel density rates, normal-reference bandwidth, the curse of dimensionality proved, learning curves of both families |
| @sec-ch-mla-nb | conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, naive Bayes; Gaussian, Bernoulli, multinomial, complement, categorical | base-rate fallacy, parameter count of the naive assumption, Laplace smoothing as a Dirichlet posterior mean, quadratic/linear boundaries, over-confidence and calibration |
| @sec-ch-mla-svm | support vector classifier, non-linear boundaries, kernels; maximal and soft margins, outliers, linear/polynomial/sigmoid/RBF kernels | margin as a convex problem with a unique solution, hinge-loss equivalence, dual and KKT, leave-one-out bound, PSD kernels, the RBF feature map, Pegasos |
| @sec-ch-mla-nn | artificial neuron, activations, multilayer perceptron, training, universal approximation | Novikoff's theorem, XOR, vanishing gradients, backpropagation derived and implemented, Glorot/He initialisation, a constructive universal approximation proof |
| @sec-ch-mla-knn | nearest neighbours, $k$-NN, distance metrics, radius neighbours | Minkowski metrics proved, scaling and Mahalanobis, choosing $k$ honestly, Cover–Hart bound, curse of dimensionality, a reject option |
| @sec-ch-mla-trees | decision trees, bias–variance, bagging, random forests | impurity concavity, best-split search from scratch, cost-complexity pruning, variance of correlated averages, out-of-bag $1/e$, MDI versus permutation importance |
| @sec-ch-mla-project | the final project | requirements, a forensic look at the data (synthetic, with inconsistencies) and a Bayes ceiling, a re-execution and code review of the published notebook, nested comparison of five models, error analysis, conclusions in plain words |

## The final project {.unnumbered}

The course ends with the **classification of fruit types from a few physical
measurements** — weight, average diameter and length, peel hardness and
sweetness — with a $k$-nearest-neighbour classifier preceded by a careful
exploratory analysis, a justified choice of $k$ and of the distance, an
evaluation on unseen data that goes beyond overall accuracy to the errors
between specific classes, and an explanation that colleagues without a
technical background can follow.

@sec-ch-mla-project states the requirements in my own words, checks in code
where the data come from and what they contain — they turn out to be
synthetic, with some impossible values — maps each requirement to the
chapters above, reviews the notebook I submitted after re-executing it, and
presents a reference implementation that compares five classifiers by nested
cross-validation against an estimate of the best achievable accuracy.
